Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who is the subject of The Beatles' song, Martha My Dear?
Answer: It’s always been said that the song is about Martha, Paul’s sheepdog. Of course, many Beatles fans assume that it has to be about something more—a relationship Paul had— perhaps the end of his relationship with Jane Asher or the beginning of his relationship with Linda Eastman. But in the 1997 McCartney biography, “Many Years From Now,” Paul confirmed the truth: “Whereas it would appear to anybody else to be a song to a girl called Martha, it’s actually a dog, and our relationship was platonic.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why did John Lennon only ever play rhythm guitar for The Beatles and occasionally, keyboards too?
Answer: John Lennon played the following instruments on various Beatles records: electric guitar, acoustic guitar, piano, electric piano, organ, harpsichord, harmonium, Mellotron, Moog synthesizer, harmonica, banjo, ukelele, bass guitar, lap steel guitar, drums, various percussion instruments and tenor sax. If you don’t count the percussion instruments, he played 16 different instruments on Beatles records. George Harrison played 14 instruments on Beatles records. Paul McCartney played 13 instruments on Beatles records. Ringo Starr played drums and numerous percussion instruments on Beatles records. He also played organ, piano and harmonica. All the Beatles were multi-instrumentalists and of the Fab Four, Lennon played the most instruments on Beatles records.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did The Beatles ever do a live album? If so, what songs were on it?
Answer: The Beatles never intentionally set out to record a live album. In January, 1979, nine years after the group broke up, an album entitled “The Beatles: Live! at the Star-Club in Hamburg Germany, 1962” appeared in the US. It had been recorded on a home tape recorder with a single microphone, so the sound quality was dreadful. It never cracked the top 100 in albums. In May, 1977, “The Beatles at the Hollywood Bowl” was released. This album was produced by George Martin, so it more or less had the stamp of approval by the group. Songs included the typical Beatles songs from their lives sets in the years 1964–65: Twist and Shout, She’s a Woman, Dizzy Miss Lizzy, Ticket to Ride, Can’t Buy Me Love, Roll Over Beethoven, Boys, Long Tall Sally, and more. The album went to #2 in the US. There are two albums produced in the 1990’s, “Live at the BBC,” Volumes 1 and 2, which also sold well.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What is the song 'Revolution #9' from The Beatles about?
Answer: “Revolution 9” is a sound collage from the “White Album.” The composition was co-created by John Lennon, Yoko Ono and George Harrison. Lennon said he was trying to paint a picture of a revolution using sound. However, the composition isn’t really “about” anything, as there is no narrative. It’s really just about the sounds. The composition was influenced by “musique concrete,” a style created by mixing recorded sounds. “Musique concrete” began to be developed in the 1940’s and was utilized by composers such as Edgard Varese and Karlheinz Stockhausen. For “Revolution 9,” George Harrison and Ringo Starr chose sounds from EMI’s tape library, including the famous “number nine, number nine” dialog. Lennon, Harrison and Ono started with a tape for a coda to “Revolution” that had been recorded by the four Beatles. They combined that with the sounds from the library, sound effects, and tape loops of speech and recorded music. Some of the loops were played backwards. Others were manipulated with echo, distortion, stereo panning, and other effects. The resulting 8:22 track is generally regarded as the Beatles’ least popular track. However, I think it’s notable that Lennon, Ono and Harrison were able to expose tens of millions of fans to avant-garde music that they wouldn’t have otherwise been exposed to. So, that’s really what “Revolution 9” was about.

Question: Why is "The Wizard of Oz" in the public domain while "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland" is not? Who owns the rights to those stories in the United States?
Answer: Both “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland” by Lewis Carroll and “The Wonderful Wizard of Oz” by L. Frank Baum have long been in the public domain. Both books are free to be used without restrictions. Alice in Wonderland was published in 1865. The Wizard of Oz was published in 1900. In the U.S., anything published prior to 1927 is in the public domain. However, the movie “The Wizard of Oz,” which was released in 1939, is NOT in the public domain and will be protected by copyright for another 12 years. The well-known movie versions of Alice in Wonderland, whether by Disney, Tim Burton or others, are also protected by copyright. When using a Public Domain writing, it’s necessary to distinguish between the original writing and a derivative work based on the original which has its own copyright.
